official_source_review.method: Targeted check of the official EUR-Lex texts and European Commission materials listed below, including the cited provisions and guidance sections.
official_source_review.reviewer_type: model-assisted maintenance cross-check; not an independent legal reviewer
official_source_review.scope: EU/common sources only. This does not check national implementation, country-specific appeal deadlines, mission arrangements, or an individual case date.
official_source_review.currentness_limit: The EUR-Lex Visa Code version list showed a consolidated text dated 2024-06-28 and amendments through Regulation (EU) 2024/1415. The reviewed VIS consolidated text is dated 2023-12-27. These dated texts must be checked against the Official Journal for later amendments, commencement and the relevant case date before substantive use. Regulation (EU) 2016/1191 was checked against its Official Journal text; EUR-Lex displayed the act as in force and its consolidated version dated 2016-07-26. Check later amendments and the applicable Member-State rules for the case date.
official_source_review.authority_limit: Regulations and directives are identified as binding EU acts. Commission notices and handbooks are non-binding guidance. CJEU judgments interpret EU law but remain subject to their facts and procedural context.
official_source_review.independent_review: Pending: an independent legal reviewer must confirm the source mapping, applicability limits, and any national-law route before these pathways support a legal merits conclusion.

topics.label: Possible obstruction before formal lodging
topics.adverse_signal: A person attempted to submit an application or required form, and an identified authority or service channel prevented acceptance before a formal decision or receipt was created.

jurisdictional_scope.eu_common: Directive 2004/38 Article 5(2) may govern an entry-visa request by a qualifying family member; otherwise the Visa Code procedure may apply. Visa Code Article 17(5) says a Member State may maintain the possibility of direct lodging at its consulate; it does not state a universal mandatory direct channel for every Member State and application.
jurisdictional_scope.national_or_local: Identify the deciding and representing Member State, local mission/service-provider arrangement, and country-specific complaint or urgent-remedy route. Verify whether the deciding or representing Member State currently maintains direct lodging, the actual appointment/intake channel, and any special EU-family procedure.

scope_questions: Was this an entry-visa application for a family member within Directive 2004/38, an ordinary Visa Code application, or another procedure?
Which state decided, represented, hosted the mission, and operated the service channel?
Was there a formal refusal, a pre-lodgement access problem, an incomplete submission, or an appointment/inquiry issue?

sources.registry_state: official_EUR-Lex_text_checked_2026-10-20; confirm applicable version and national implementation for case date

provisions: Article 17(5): a Member State may maintain direct lodging at its consulate; verify the actual State route
sources.registry_state: official_consolidation_2024-06-28_checked_2026-10-20; amendment and case-date check required

provisions: Part II, sections 2.2.1-2.2.2; Part III for EU-family safeguards
sources.registry_state: Commission C(2024) 4319 final checked 2026-10-20; nonbinding guidance; verify later replacement

counterarguments_and_exceptions: A request to use an appointment, provide a complete form, attend biometrics, or approach a competent mission is not automatically a refusal to lodge.
A service provider may perform limited intake tasks under an applicable arrangement; examination and decision remain with the consulate under the Visa Code.
The authority, procedure, urgency, representation arrangement, and any usable alternative channel may change the analysis.

Visa Code Article 17(5) permits a Member State to maintain a direct-lodging possibility; do not turn that wording into a universal direct-lodging entitlement. Article 43(6) permits specified provider intake/logistics, while Article 43(4) reserves examination and decisions to the consulate.
records_to_seek: Dated lodging attempt and exact form/version
Written instructions or refusal, including sender and authority role
Portal status, receipt, appointment record, and subsequent correspondence
Available alternative channel and any access or accessibility barrier
Current deciding/representing Member State instructions showing whether direct consular lodging is maintained, provider tasks, appointment channel, and any refusal or alternative offered
topics.possible_next_step: Identify the deciding and representing Member States, then ask the competent mission to confirm whether direct lodging is maintained under Visa Code Article 17(5), which appointment/intake steps a provider performs, and the route for any refusal to accept an application.
topics.remedy_competence_and_limits: The national competent authority and urgent judicial route are not resolved by this shared EU review record. Do not describe a pre-lodgement access problem as a formal refusal without evidence. Article 17(5) does not establish a universal direct-channel obligation; check the current Member-State arrangement and any separate Directive-based facilitation requirement.

topics.label: Digital-only or service-provider access requirement
topics.adverse_signal: A digital platform, VAC, or intermediary is said to be the only way to request or lodge, and the person reports being unable to use it or reach an effective alternative.

jurisdictional_scope.eu_common: Visa Code Articles 9-11 and 43-45 govern relevant short-stay visa channels; Regulation (EU) 2023/2667 creates a staged EU Visa Application Platform framework.
jurisdictional_scope.national_or_local: Check the platform's operational start decision, any Member-State transition opt-out, local appointment channel, accessibility arrangements, and national accessibility remedies.

scope_questions: Is the platform mandatory at the relevant date and for this application type?
Is the intermediary acting as an external service provider, commercial intermediary, or merely an optional channel?
Which state decides, which mission represents it, and which authority handles data and lodging?

sources.registry_state: official_consolidation_2024-06-28_checked_2026-10-20; amendment and case-date check required

provisions: Article 7: EU VAP start requires a separate Commission decision; Member States may notify a transition opt-out of up to seven years
sources.registry_state: Official Journal text checked 2026-10-20; not in pinned core pack; check start decision and Member-State notice at case date

provisions: Part II, section 2.2.1: urgent appointment/direct access; section 2.2.2: appointment timing
sources.registry_state: Commission C(2024) 4319 final checked 2026-10-20; nonbinding guidance; verify later replacement

counterarguments_and_exceptions: Visa Code Article 10(1) permits electronic lodgement where available, while personal appearance may be required for fingerprint collection; assess the actual route and exceptions.

Regulation (EU) 2023/2667 Article 7 makes EU VAP operation dependent on a Commission start-date decision and permits Member-State transition opt-outs; do not infer a live or exclusive EU-wide platform from the regulation alone.

External service providers may perform specified intake tasks, but examination and the visa decision remain with the consulate under Article 43(4); a service-provider logistics requirement does not itself establish unlawful access.
records_to_seek: Exact platform message and date
Published instructions and version
Alternative or assisted channel and response
Any representation arrangement, accessibility need, or failed upload record
topics.possible_next_step: Ask the deciding mission to identify the governing route and an accessible alternative; preserve screenshots and dated access errors.
topics.remedy_competence_and_limits: No general illegality inference follows from a digital process. Competence, commencement, alternatives, and national accessibility remedies require separate checking.

topics.label: EU-family proof and ordinary Schengen checklist
topics.adverse_signal: An authority is reported to reject or refuse to consider relevant evidence of EU-citizen identity, family relationship, dependency, or accompanying/joining because it is not on a stated list.

jurisdictional_scope.eu_common: First establish whether Directive 2004/38 applies; where it does, Commission guidance says applicants may choose relevant proof of family relationship and other covered conditions. Regulation (EU) 2016/1191 may remove legalisation/apostille formalities for covered public documents issued by one Member State for presentation in another; it does not decide recognition of the document's legal effects.
jurisdictional_scope.national_or_local: Verify local instructions and any national evidential rules without treating an ordinary Schengen checklist as a closed EU-family proof rule. Confirm that the issuing authority/document/purpose and receiving Member State meet the Regulation's scope, and check translation/certified-copy rules plus any national assessment of legal effects.

scope_questions: Does Directive 2004/38 apply to this EU citizen and family member on these facts?
What proposition must be proved, what evidence was offered, and what did the authority actually reject?
Is the list binding, exhaustive, illustrative, or an ordinary Visa Code list applied in a different scope?

official_consolidation_2024-06-28_checked_2026-10-20; amendment and case-date check required

provisions: Section 2.2.4: relevant alternative evidence may not be refused solely because it is not the preferred document type

provisions: Part III: assess the Visa Code together with the specific Directive/Withdrawal Agreement rules for eligible family members
sources.registry_state: Commission C(2024) 4319 final checked 2026-10-20; nonbinding guidance; verify later replacement

provisions: Article 2(3)(a)-(b) (third-country documents and Member-State-certified copies of them excluded)
Article 4 (exemption from legalisation and similar formality)
sources.registry_state: Official Journal text checked 2026-10-20; not in pinned core pack; applies only to covered public documents issued by one Member State for presentation in another; verify amendments, document scope, translation rules and case-date national treatment

counterarguments_and_exceptions: A checklist can be illustrative or request evidence relevant to the actual eligibility condition.
Alternative evidence can be considered and still found insufficient for a stated, evidence-based reason.
The Directive's scope and relationship with the Visa Code must be established before importing its family-member facilitation rules.

For a covered public document establishing marriage, Regulation (EU) 2016/1191 can exempt the document from legalisation or an apostille when presented in another Member State; it does not require recognition of the legal effects of its contents or establish every family-member eligibility condition.

For a covered document, Article 5 limits demands for both an original and certified copy and requires acceptance of a certified copy made in another Member State when certified copies are permitted; Article 6(1) limits translation demands in the stated language or sufficient multilingual-form conditions. Check the exact form, accepted languages and receiving-state procedure.
records_to_seek: Exact checklist and any statement that it is exhaustive
Identity/family evidence actually presented
Authority response and reason for rejecting any alternative
Facts establishing the EU citizen's movement and the applicant's claimed category
Issuing authority and Member State, receiving authority and Member State, document purpose and form
Any translation, multilingual standard form, certified-copy, authenticity, or separate legal-effect objection

If relevant, whether the authority permits a certified copy, the issuing state of that copy, the document language, any accepted-language list, and whether a multilingual standard form contains enough information
topics.possible_next_step: Identify the issuing and receiving Member States and exact document purpose; check whether Regulation (EU) 2016/1191 applies to formalities, then assess any separate translation, evidential, or legal-effect issue under the responsible national rules.
topics.remedy_competence_and_limits: The pathway flags a proof issue for review. It does not establish family status, documentary sufficiency, or an unlawful closed list. Commission guidance is nonbinding. Regulation (EU) 2016/1191 is limited to covered Member-State public documents and formalities; it excludes third-country public documents and does not determine recognition of legal effects. A document falling outside it may still be governed by another treaty or national rule, so do not assume an apostille is always required.

topics.label: Complaint, appeal, or review-path information
topics.adverse_signal: A formal decision or independently actionable procedural act is known, but the authority's review information or the actual route is reported missing, inaccessible, or contradictory.

jurisdictional_scope.eu_common: Visa Code Article 32(3) requires a right of appeal under national law; Directive 2004/38 Article 31 and Charter Article 47 may apply within their respective scopes.
jurisdictional_scope.national_or_local: The competent court/authority, deadline, filing method, standing and interim relief must be checked in the current national procedure for the actual decision and service date.

scope_questions: Was a formal appealable decision issued, or is the concern an earlier service/access problem?
Which decision-maker and legal regime apply?
What review route exists in the relevant national system and what deadline applies?

provisions: Article 38(5): Member States must provide a complaint procedure for staff conduct/application process and make its information public
sources.registry_state: official_consolidation_2024-06-28_checked_2026-10-20; amendment and case-date check required
official_EUR-Lex_text_checked_2026-10-20; national remedy remains unverified

provisions: Article 47, only within the Charter's Article 51 scope
sources.registry_state: Official Journal text checked 2026-10-20; applicability depends on implementation of EU law

provisions: Part II, section 11.2; Part III family-member appeal information
sources.registry_state: Commission C(2024) 4319 final checked 2026-10-20; points to national appeal law; nonbinding

counterarguments_and_exceptions: A complaint route can exist elsewhere in the legal system even if a web page omits it.
An informal complaint, supervisory route, SOLVIT, and judicial appeal are distinct and may not suspend one another's deadlines.
A procedural step may not be a separately reviewable decision at the current stage.

Visa Code Article 38(5) requires a procedure for complaints about staff conduct or the application process and public information about that procedure. A missing website link therefore does not alone prove the procedure is unavailable; this complaint process is distinct from the appeal right for a visa refusal under Article 32(3).
records_to_seek: Decision and service date
Appeal instructions and envelope/portal timestamp
Current official national procedure and competent court/authority
Any separate service complaint and whether it affects a deadline
Official national complaint procedure, authoritative decision instructions, alternate official publication of the route, and whether the complaint affects any appeal deadline
topics.possible_next_step: Check the current official decision instructions and national procedure for the exact complaint or appeal sought; distinguish a website omission, an Article 38(5) staff/process complaint, and a formal visa-refusal appeal.
topics.remedy_competence_and_limits: The shared record cannot identify a national court, filing method, deadline, or interim remedy without a current Member-State source pack and case-stage facts. Article 38(5) requires a complaint procedure and public information, but it does not itself identify a country-specific filing body, deadline, judicial remedy, or suspensive effect.

topics.label: Appointment access and processing clock
topics.adverse_signal: A dated appointment or processing delay is reported, with a potentially applicable statutory or accelerated time rule.

jurisdictional_scope.eu_common: Visa Code Article 9(2)-(3) concerns appointment access; Article 23 processing time begins when an admissible application is lodged. Directive Article 5(2) adds accelerated handling for qualifying EU-family entry visas.
jurisdictional_scope.national_or_local: Verify local appointment channels, representation and case-date rules; national urgent remedies and service standards require the responsible Member-State source.

scope_questions: Was an appointment requested, an application formally lodged, or only an inquiry submitted?
Which legal clock applies and what event starts it?
Is an EU-family accelerated procedure engaged, and what exact current authority source governs the step?

sources.registry_state: official_consolidation_2024-06-28_checked_2026-10-20; appointment and processing clocks differ; amendment check required
official_EUR-Lex_text_checked_2026-10-20; qualifying-family-member and urgency conditions matter

provisions: Part II, section 2.2.2: appointment generally within two weeks; Part III, section 4.4: EU-family processing beyond 15 days exceptional and duly justified, delays beyond four weeks described as not reasonable
sources.registry_state: Commission C(2024) 4319 final checked 2026-10-20; nonbinding guidance, not a freestanding statutory deadline; verify later replacement

counterarguments_and_exceptions: Appointment waiting time is not automatically the same clock as processing after lodging.
Urgency, appointment availability, completeness, representation, and justified extensions may matter.
A missed service target does not by itself establish an individual remedy or damages claim.
records_to_seek: Appointment request and response dates
Formal lodging receipt and any later completeness notice
Applicable current rule, start event, pauses, extensions, and decision service date
Urgency evidence and any alternative appointment offered
topics.possible_next_step: Build a dated chronology with each event labelled separately and verify the exact current deadline rule before describing it as overdue.
topics.remedy_competence_and_limits: The core pattern is a review hypothesis only; it does not calculate a national urgent remedy or infer lateness from today's date.

topics.label: Personal-data access, minimisation, and separate preservation request
topics.adverse_signal: A specific personal-data request or a narrowly identified record-preservation concern is reported, with a named or potentially identifiable controller/processor and purpose.

jurisdictional_scope.eu_common: GDPR rights and the VIS Regulation may cover defined personal-data processing; CJEU case law construes the GDPR copy right.
jurisdictional_scope.national_or_local: Identify each controller and applicable data regime; national administrative-file access, secrecy restrictions, supervisory procedure and any preservation order remain separate questions.

scope_questions: Which entity determines the processing purpose and means?
Does GDPR apply, or does a specialized Visa Information System or law-enforcement regime govern some data?
Is the request for personal data under GDPR Article 15 or for a whole administrative case file under national procedure?
Is preservation being requested under an identified legal basis or only as a practical step?

sources.registry_state: Official Journal text checked 2026-10-20; controller, processing purpose, special regimes and any restriction law require verification

provisions: Articles 38-40: VIS rights, assistance and remedies
sources.registry_state: official_consolidation_2023-12-27 checked 2026-10-20; not in pinned core pack; verify amendments and regime applicability

provisions: Case C-487/21, paragraphs 39-44: context can require document extracts or entire documents for an intelligible copy, subject to others' rights; no general full-file entitlement
sources.registry_state: Official CJEU judgment checked 2026-10-20; apply only to the GDPR access issue and relevant facts

counterarguments_and_exceptions: Article 15 concerns personal data and prescribed information. Under C-487/21, document extracts or entire documents may be needed where essential for intelligibility, subject to others' rights; this is not a general full-file entitlement.

Article 18(1)(c) restriction is available only where the controller no longer needs the data but the data subject needs them for legal claims; Article 17(3)(e) can limit erasure where processing is needed for legal claims.
Article 23 restrictions require a legislative measure meeting its conditions; do not infer a restriction without identifying that measure.
VIS access, correction and remedies have specialized provisions; a practical preservation request is distinct from an automatic retention duty or judicial preservation order.
records_to_seek: Targeted request, response, identity verification, and delivery evidence
Controller/processor identity and processing purpose
Specific data categories, systems, recipients, and date range
Separate preservation request, records at risk, and any national procedural basis
topics.possible_next_step: Separate the data-subject access request from any administrative-file request and any preservation request; identify the controller and ask for the applicable review route.
topics.remedy_competence_and_limits: No automatic deletion, retention, full-file access, or preservation conclusion. National access-to-file rules and specialized visa-data procedures remain separate source tasks.
